passage_text: Researchers investigated the effect of four different cognitive training protocols (A, B, C, and D) on reaction time in a visual search task. Thirty participants were randomly assigned to each protocol. After a 4‑week training period, participants completed a standardized reaction‑time test. The mean reaction times (in seconds) and standard deviations (SD) for each protocol are shown in Table 1. The data suggest that protocol B produced the fastest reaction times, while protocol C was the slowest. The researchers plan to use these findings to recommend a protocol for clinical rehabilitation programs targeting patients with slowed processing speeds.
table_data:
Treatment | Sample Size | Mean Response Time (s) | SD
A | 30 | 12.5 | 2.3
B | 30 | 10.8 | 1.9
C | 30 | 13.2 | 2.1
D | 30 | 11.5 | 2.0
stem: Based on Table 1, which protocol yielded the fastest mean reaction time?
explanation: Protocol B has the lowest mean reaction time (10.8 s) compared with A (12.5 s), C (13.2 s), and D (11.5 s).
trap: Reading the highest mean (Protocol C, 13.2 s) as the best result, when a lower mean reaction time means a faster response.

stem: Which experimental design would best determine whether the observed differences in reaction time are caused by the training protocols?

options.A: Cross‑sectional survey of participants’ self‑reported training history
options.B: Randomized controlled trial with double‑blinded assessment
options.C: Case‑control study comparing trained vs. untrained individuals
options.D: Longitudinal cohort study following participants for 10 years

explanation: A randomized controlled trial with double‑blinded assessment controls for confounders and bias, allowing causal inference about the effect of each protocol on reaction time.
trap: Choosing a case‑control design, which is better for rare outcomes rather than comparing interventions.

stem: What is the percent improvement in mean reaction time when comparing protocol B to protocol A?
explanation: Correct: A) (12.5 − 10.8)/12.5 × 100 = 1.7/12.5 × 100 = 13.6%. Why the others are wrong: B) 15.7% divides the 1.7 s difference by protocol B's mean (10.8 s) instead of protocol A's baseline. C) 17.5% does not follow from the 1.7 s difference and either mean. D) 19.2% divides the B-versus-C difference (2.4 s) by protocol A's mean, comparing the wrong protocols.
trap: Dividing the 1.7 s difference by protocol B's mean (10.8 s) instead of protocol A's gives 15.7% (option B); the baseline protocol A must be the denominator.

stem: Which of the following is a common misinterpretation of the data presented in Table 1?

options.A: Protocol B had the lowest mean response time.
options.B: Protocol A had a larger SD than protocol B.
options.C: Protocol C’s higher mean suggests it is the most effective
options.D: Protocol C had the highest mean response time.

explanation: A higher mean reaction time indicates slower responses, so protocol C is actually the least effective, not the most.
trap: Assuming that a higher mean always reflects better performance.
